Having adorned it with eight banners, with Hari seated upon it, decorated with royal swans, fish, and silk ribbons and garlands.

Above, it is adorned with eight banners: lions, peacocks, swans, and the king of makaras; it is further embellished with five-fold silk garlands. Having laid down two Brahma-lines, the wise one should cast two diagonal lines toward the four directions, as well as another line for the door.
The intelligent one should strike the two Brahma-lines at the four corners, and from those, the other door-lines should be struck.
The Vajrācārya, being well-composed, should lay down the root-lines; by means of a sixfold division of the circle, the door becomes beautiful.
The Vajra Master, remaining in meditative equipoise, should strike the primary lines; by means of six parts of the wheel, the gates will become beautiful.
One should designate the ground for the colored powders (rajobhūmi) as one-fifth of the door's width; its measure should be equal to that, and the altar (vedikā) should be twice that.
The ground for the colored powders should be carefully measured using five parts of the door; its dimensions shall be equal, and the pedestal should be made twice that size.
The fourth [line] should be with half of the vedikā; of this there is no doubt. The fifth is equal to the vedikā, and the sixth and seventh are each half of that.
The fourth, by half of the pedestal, becomes the line for the precious cloth; the fifth is equal to the pedestal; the sixth and seventh are half of that.
Outside the door-line, on the left and right sides, one should drop six lines each for the three Adhityās.
Outside the lines of the door, having set aside one measure each on the left and right sides, one should strike the lines for the six panels.
Having moved sixteen measures outward from the seventh line, one should bend the cord into a circle, equal in extent to the pericarp.
Outside the seventh line, one should discard a measure of sixteen; this is the summary of the meaning of the circular perimeter line and the navel.
Then, having discarded three measures, one should draw the lotus thread. Then, having discarded two measures, one should draw the vajra-garland.
Then, having set aside three measures, one should encircle it with the lotus lines. Then, having set aside two measures, one should encircle it with the vajra garland.
There, having set aside two measures, one should trace the vajra garland; then, having set aside four measures, one should trace the circle of flames.
Then, having set aside four measures, one should surround [the area] with a garland of flames.
Outside of that, for five measures, is the ground of Asitāṅga and the others; outside of that, for ten measures, the cremation grounds are prescribed.
Outside of that, by five measures, [one forms] the non-white limbs and so forth; outside of that, by those same measures, it is held to be the ground of the charnel grounds (*śmaśāna*).
Outside of that, the ground of the row of skull-bowls (*kapālāvalī*) shall consist of three *mātrikās*. By eight measures of the outer maṇḍala, there is the inner maṇḍala.
Outside of that, by the garland of skulls, it becomes three measures. By the measures of the outer maṇḍala, the eight [measures] constitute the heart maṇḍala.
The wise one should lay down the root-lines in the four directions; by means of a fifth part of that, the measurement for the doorways is established.
The wise one should strike the root lines in four squares; the area of five parts of that shall become the lines of the gates.

The measurement of that [door] is declared to be twenty-six units (mātrās). It is explained that the ground consists of five squares; the wise should strike the lines there. Having abandoned a measure of two [units] outside of that, one should strike the lines for the pedestal (*vedikā*).

Having abandoned the outer *mātrikā*, one should strike the lines for the frieze (*paṭṭikā*). Outside of that, the measurement of the pedestal is according to the dimensions of the hanging-frieze (*hārapaṭṭi*).

Outside of that, having set aside one measure, there is the line for the jewel-strip (*bakulī*). Outside of that, there is the measure for the pedestal; it becomes the measure for the necklace-strip (*paṭṭikā*).

Outside of that, at a distance of one unit and then another unit, there are two *iṣṭakā* [intervals], which constitute the *puṣpa-paṭṭikā*.
On both sides, outside the door-line (*dvārasūtra*), the wise one should cast six lines each, separated by one unit.

Outside the lines of the door, starting from one unit and ending at the next, the wise one should strike the lines for the cloth on both sides. Hereafter, I shall explain the drawing of the central maṇḍala; one should preserve the third line within the root lines.

In each of the [four] directions, starting with the northeast and so forth, one should arrange the seats such as the lion and others; likewise, in due order, the elephant, peacock, and garuda, as well as the commissioned attendants. One should designate the lion, boar, buffalo, and jackal as the seats; at the four gates, one should fashion the corpse-seats for the goddesses.
One should arrange the seats of the lion, the boar, the buffalo, and the jackal; the four goddesses should be visualized as having corpses for their seats.
Outside the vajra-prākāra, one should meditate on twenty lotus-moons as the seats, adorned with mandalas red as blood.
Outside the vajra fence, upon a mandala red as blood, one should visualize twenty lotuses and moons as their seats.
Outside that, in a circle, on a wheel brilliant with a golden luster, are twenty lotuses and moons for Karaṅka, Bhairava, and the others.
Its exterior is circular, with a golden-colored perimeter blazing all around; upon twenty lotuses and moon disks are [the deities] such as Keng rus (Kankāla) and A jigs byed (Bhīṣaṇa).
One should visualize their respective seats at the outer doors and corners: Garuḍa, as well as the Haṃsa, the Bull, and the Elephant, in due order.
One should visualize those born from the breath at the outer gates and corners, in the sequence of the garuḍa, the swan, the bull, and the elephant.
One should visualize Erāvata, a man, a dog, and likewise a makara. In the center, arisen from the seed-syllable and the emblem, is the Lord Yogāmbara.
One should meditate on the earth, the man, the horse, and the makara itself; in the center, arisen from the seed-syllable and the emblem, is the Lord of the Yogins of Space.
One should meditate with one's entire being, characterized by the previously mentioned signs; [one should meditate on] the Hero whose nature is wisdom and means, the leader of the circle of Yoginīs.
*One should meditate on all things, as indicated by the very characteristics mentioned before; one should become the essence of wisdom and means, the sovereign of the circle of Yoginīs.*
Having meditated on the complete mandala within his heart with a concentrated mind, he should emit the deities of the mandala in their proper order by means of their respective seed-syllables.

Perfectly complete with all ornaments, one should visualize them at the heart while in meditative equipoise; then, according to their respective seed-syllables, the maṇḍalas should be emanated in sequence.
Vajrī, Ghorī, Vetālī, and Caṇḍālī are also [the consorts] of the yogins; having thus accomplished the welfare of the world, he should cause them to be seated upon their respective seats.
Having brought forth from their breath the fierce Vajrī, the Vetālī, the Caṇḍālī, and the Yoginīs, they should perform the benefit of beings and then be established [within].
Having generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) and bestowed the vision of primordial wisdom, she is the bestower of the Buddha’s enlightenment upon the eightfold noble path.
One should generate the mind of awakening, which bestows the vision of primordial wisdom; it grants the eightfold path of omniscience and the supreme awakening of a Buddha.
To the front, to the left, to the back, and likewise to the right— white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black—
with four arms and a fierce form.

Lalita, with her lotus posture, her crown, and her knees resting upon her seat; with hair flowing loose, she remains embracing her own *kuleśa* (Lord of the Family) in union. With her right hand she holds lotus vessels, and with her left she carries a *khaṭvāṅga*. She is draped in human skin, and her lower garment is made of elephant hide.
Holding a lotus vessel with her right hand and grasping a khaṭvāṅga with her left, she covers her upper body with human skin and wears an elephant hide as a lower garment;
her entire body is adorned with all ornaments and her eyes are radiant. In the northeast is the goddess Śrīherukī, emanated from the syllable ŚRĪM.
Upon her body are all eyes, and she is adorned with three eyes. The goddess Indrāṇī Siṃhikā is manifested upon the water-pile (vāri-kaṭāha).
She is white and yellow in color, standing in a graceful posture (*lalitākṣepa*). Her face is adorned with playful ornaments, she has three eyes, and she possesses a wrathful form.
Her complexion is white and yellow; she stands in a playful stance. Her face has bared fangs, and she has the appearance of a wrathful deity with three eyes.
In her right hand she brandishes a sword, and in her left she holds a noose with the threatening gesture; she is well-draped in red garments and adorned with all ornaments.
With the right hand, he holds a sword aloft; with the left, he displays the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*). He is well-dressed in red robes and adorned with all the ornaments.
The goddess Vyāghriṇī, born from the peak of the earth, dwells in the southeast; she consumes all Māras and possesses a radiance equal to a blazing flame of fire.
With a radiance like a blazing fire, she consumes all the Māras; in the midst of that fire, the goddess Vyāghrī has truly emerged upon a mound of earth.
White and blue in color, she stands in the *maṇḍala* posture; she has two arms, a loud laugh, and is adorned with three eyes.
White and blue in color, she stands in the *maṇḍala* posture; she has two arms, a loud laugh, and is adorned with three eyes.
Holding a hook, a threatening gesture, and a noose, adorned with red garments, the goddess Jambukī arises from Vāyukūṭa in the south-western direction (Nairṛtya).

Her body is blue and red in color, adorned with three eyes. She is perfectly endowed with excellent ornaments; in her right hand she holds a battle-axe, and in her left, the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and a noose. Seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), she is decorated with red garments. And in the northwest is Urukīnī, who has arisen from fire.
Seated perfectly in the half-lotus posture, adorned with red robes, she emerged from a mass of fire in the southwest direction as an owl.
Having a complexion of reddish-yellow, she is seated in the utkuṭaka posture; she is adorned with three eyes and holds a staff, a threatening gesture, and a noose.
With all her limbs adorned with ornaments and beautifully decorated with red garments, she is the Ḍākinī at the eastern gate, arisen from the seed-syllable *phuṃ*.
White in color with great flames, adorned with disheveled hair, she casts [the victim] into her mouth with both hands, beautifully adorned with three eyes.
Greatly blazing with white color, adorned with loose locks of hair, with both hands placed in the mouth, and beautifully adorned with three eyes.

Well-draped in red garments and seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, the Ḍākinī, born from the seed-syllable *Phūṃ*, is at the eastern gate. In the north is the goddess Dīpinī, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture; she is yellow in color, possesses great radiance, and is adorned with all ornaments.

In the north is the goddess Dīpā, seated perfectly in the bodhisattva posture. She is of great yellow radiance, adorned with all ornaments, well-clad in red garments, and resplendent with three eyes. Born from the seed-syllable PHĪṂ, she holds her hands joined in *añjali* at her crown.
She is well-adorned with red garments [... born from the seed-syllable YAṂ, with palms joined and placed upon her crown.
At the western gate is Cūṣiṇī, of red color and great brilliance; she drinks [blood] from a cupped handful, being emanated by the syllable PHOṂ.
At the western gate is Bhīmā, red in color and greatly terrifying; blood flows from her nostrils, and she is emanated from the syllable *praṃ*.
At the southern gate is Kāmbojī, black in color and possessing great laughter; holding a pestle in her two hands, she is produced from the syllable *phiṃ*.
At the southern gate is Hārītī, black in color and greatly blazing; she holds a pestle in her two hands and is emanated from the syllable PHREṂ.
Outside the vajra-fence, those emanated from the seed-syllables HAḤ, HOḤ, HRĪḤ, and BĪ are to be visualized. One should visualize Pukkasī, Ḍrāmiḍī, and Caṇḍī in the eastern direction.
Outside the vajra fence, emanated from the seed-syllables HAḤ HOḤ HRĪḤ, one should meditate on the three—Guptā, Ājū, and Caṇḍālī—in the eastern direction.
White, blue, and golden in appearance, they are adorned with three eyes; with their two hands, they hold vessels of ambrosial nectar resting upon wheels.
With three eyes, he is adorned with white, blue, and yellow colors; with two hands resting upon a skull-cup, he holds the drink of nectar.

Ghorī, Rudharī, and Māṃsī reside in the northern direction; their colors are yellow, white, and ruddy, and they are born from the seed-syllables GHRĪṂ and GHRĀḤ. Dragmo, Khrag-’thung, and Sha-gsol-ma dwell in the northern quarter; their colors are yellow, white, and red, and they arise from the seed-syllables GHRĪṂ and GHRĀḤ. Holding a five-pronged hook, a full lotus, and a vessel, they sit upon a being in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, adorned with three eyes.

Holding a supreme lotus vessel filled with the five iron hooks, seated upon the *vīrāsana* posture, and adorned with three jackals, Ugrī, Jvalitī, Bhībhatsī, and Paścimā are the Yoginīs in the western direction. Terrible, holding a vessel for offerings (*balibhāṇḍa*), they arise from the seed-syllable "Kuru."
The yoginīs of the western direction are the fierce, blazing, and unlovely ones; holding in their hands vessels of terrifying offerings, they arise from the seed-syllable *kuru*.
Radiant in red and yellow garments, they wear crowns of skulls and sit in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, adorned with three eyes.
Red, yellow, and the color of the sky, adorned with a crown of skulls, seated upon the posture of a hero (vīrāsana), and beautifully embellished with three eyes.
Kapālī, Vajriṇī, and Kumbhī reside completely in the southern direction; born from the three *varttali*, they hold skull-cups for food and drink.
With blue, red, and white radiance, seated upon a hero’s posture (sattvaparyaṅka), one should place Lāsyā in the northeast, born from the seed-syllable *Hūṃ*.
With blue, red, and white light, seated on a hero’s posture, one should place Lāsyā in the northeast, arisen from the seed-syllable *Hūṃ*.
Extremely beautiful and yellow in color, she stands with her two hips perfectly aligned; she should be placed to his left, the Goddess of Fragrance, endowed with a fragrant conch.
Of white color and most beautiful, born from the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, she who resides in the southeast is the Vīṇā goddess; intent upon playing the lute, she should be established there.
She is red, extremely beautiful, and born from the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*. Residing in the southeast is the Vīṇā goddess; that lute is the supreme of sounds.
Born from the seed-syllables *Hūṃ* and *Hoḥ*, she is white in color and charming; one should place her to his left, adorned with flowers and beautiful flower-offerings (*puṣpāñjali*).
Born from the seed-syllables *Hūṃ* and *Hoḥ*, She is white in color and delightful; The Flower Goddess resides to the left of Fire, Exceedingly beautiful with handfuls of flowers.

Born from the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, she is intensely radiant with the color of water. One should place the Nāginī of the South-West, who is intensely radiant with a blue color. Born from the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, she is intensely radiant with a blue color; the Nāginī dwelling in the direction of Nirṛti is intensely radiant with a blue color.
Born from the utterance of *hūṃ hūṃ*, she is sung of by Śvetācāla; one should place the incense burner, beautiful with its red color, to her left.

Born from the syllable *hūṃ hūṃ*, she is white and performs a dance while singing. To her left stands Dhūpā, red in color and lovely; born from the seed-syllable *i*, she holds an incense burner. In the northwest stands Nṛtyā, red in color and charming; born from the seed-syllable *i*, she holds an incense burner in her hand. This dancing goddess situated in the wind [direction] is red in color and lovely.
Born from the seed-syllable *HŪṂ*, she performs a dance with her two hands. One should place the goddess Dīpā, blazing with a yellow color, upon her left side.
Born from the seed-syllable *KṢUṂ*, she holds a lamp-staff (*dīpayaṣṭi*). On the outer circular pedestals, one should arrange the skeletons and other [emblems].
Born from the seed-syllable KṢUṂ, together with a lamp-offering pillar, one should arrange the skeletons and so forth upon the outer circular seats.
[They are] arisen from their respective seed-syllables, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture. All the heroes have four arms and wear skulls as their crest-ornaments.
Arisen from their respective seed-syllables, Seated with the sattvaparyaṅka posture, All the heroes have four arms, And wear skulls as their crest-ornaments.
Their hair is tied up in a yellowish-brown topknot, and they are adorned with three eyes. With a skull-cup in their right hand, they embrace the Goddess from the left.
Their hair is tied up in a yellowish-brown topknot; they are beautifully adorned with three eyes; in their right hand they hold a skull-cup, and with their left they embrace the Goddess.

Holding a *khaṭvāṅga* in the right hand and a trident raised upward in the left; all the goddesses, however, have two arms, and their colors and seed-syllables are identical to those of the Lord. [Right hand: *Khaṭvāṅga*; [Left hand: Holding a trident upward. All the goddesses have two hands; their colors, seed-syllables, and lights are the same.
Embracing the Hero with her left hand, she holds a skull-cup in her right. Born from the syllable *kaṃ* in the east is the auspicious Karaṅkabhairava;
he embraces the Hero with his right hand, while his left hand holds a skull-cup. Born from the syllable *kaṃ* in the east is that non-white, terrifying Skeleton;
born from *kaṃkāra*, she rests upon the lotus of her Lord’s body. In the second position to the right is a white lotus, together with a white *khaṭvāṅga*.

The Mother, whose form is that of a lotus, arises from the syllable *kaṃ*. To the second [lotus] on the right is Padmāvatī; the Rākṣasī Khaṭvāṅgā is born from the seed-syllable *khaṃ*, and her emblem is Kharanakhī. On the third [lotus] to the left is Gambhīranādita; she is born from the seed-syllable *gaṃ*. In her embrace is Tīkṣṇatuṇḍā, who is produced from the seed-syllable *khaṃ*. On the third [lotus] to the left...
To his left resides she who possesses a white and deep resonance, born from the seed-syllable *ghaṃ*. To the north is Ghaṇṭakarṇaka;

her sound is born from *gaṃ*. She dwells upon a lotus to his left, white in color and with a deep voice. To the north stands she who is yellow, proclaiming *ghavaṃ* by means of the syllable *ghaṃ*. One should place the yellow Vajracaṇḍaśvara in the second position to the right.

Born from the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, she stands upon his thighs. Yellow in color and born from *ghaṃ*, she is Ghaṇṭānādā (Bell-Sound). Second, arranged to the right, is the goddess embraced by him; she is Cañcalānanī, born from the seed-syllable *caṃ*. Third, on the left, is a lotus; from the syllable *chi* comes Chidrāghoṇakā. Born from *caṃ*, she is the yellow Caṇḍeśvarī; the goddess who embraces her is also born from *caṃ*, Padmānanā (Lotus-Faced). Third, on the left lotus—

Seated upon her lap is the yellow goddess Chiñjātā, who rends with her fangs; in the west is the red-colored one named Jalāyujapriyā. From the seed-syllable *tshṃ* arises a yellow bow; seated upon her lap is the yellow goddess Tshṃjātā, who rends with her fangs. In the west is the red-colored one born from the seed-syllable *jaṃ*, whose breasts are firm and high. To the second right is a lotus, radiant with the syllables *jhaja-jhaṃ*.

The one named Mngal-skyes-dga’ (Garbhajā-prīti) is born from the seed-syllable *dza*; she who dwells on her lap has a prominent nape and is red in color, known by the name Jhakṛtakāminī. On the second lotus, that of the right, is the one born from the seed-syllable *ṭi*, possessing the form of *ṭili* and terrifying with the syllable *dzheṃ*; she who dwells on her lap is red in color and is named Dza-byed-dga’-ba-mo (Jha-kārī-prīti). On the third lotus, that of the left—

Seated upon her lap is the red Līlā, whose seed-syllable is *ṭha*; she is adorned with a skull-bowl (*ṭikka*). In the southern central lotus, the seed-syllable *ṭhī* produces Ṭhīvanāṅgara; his seed-syllable is *ṭī*, and he eats the water-crystal (*chu skyar*). Seated upon her lap is the red Dhakkakāminī, whose seed-syllable is *ṭha*; she is adorned with a skull-bowl (*ṭhikka*). In the second southern lotus, the seed-syllable *ḍra* produces Ḍramaradrāmara.
Seated upon her lap is she who is blue-limbed and fond of the hand-drum (ḍiṇḍima); in the third left lotus is Ḍhañja, holding a ḍhakkā drum, a kolo, and a plowshare.

She emerges from the seed-syllable *Ḍaṃ* and subdues all; her abode is a pig, and her limbs are green. She delights in the sound of the lute (*jā*). On the third [petal], on the left lotus, she sits upon her lap, blue-bodied and fond of the *ḍhakka* drum. On the northeast and the southern lotus, one should place *Taṃja*, the beloved of *Taṅka*.
Dhā is Mahādundubhi, who possesses spectacles; her lap-dweller is Avalokita with green limbs. On the right lotus of Īśāna is Mṛdaṅgavādinī;
seated upon her lap is Tanujayinī, yellow in luster. There, on the left lotus, is the seed-syllable THO, the firm speaker.

One should visualize that man as one who delights in dispute; seated upon his lap is Śukravarṇā Tharaṅgiṇī, born from the *stana* (breast) of the donor. Upon the lotus to her left, in the southeast petal of the wheel, one should behold [the deity].

Extending her long arms from the seed-syllable *tho*, she who dwells upon his lap is Daradarśinī, white in color; on the lotus to the right of the fire [deity] is she seated upon his lap, white in luster and gazing intensely. Right there, on the lotus to the left, is the seed-syllable *dhīṃ* of Ghoraka.

The one with curved fangs born from *daṃ*, and the white one seated upon her lap; the light born from *daṃ* is *mā*. Upon her left lotus is she who has a blue complexion and speaks like a hero (*vīrabhāṣiṇī*). In the south, on the lotus of the Nairṛti direction, is the one who moves about like a mass of saffron; born from *dhiṃ*, he is firm and terrifying. Seated upon his lap is she who has blue light and speaks like a *dala*. On the lotus to the right of the Nairṛti direction—
And seated upon his lap is Piṅgalākiṇī, who has the luster of a sapphire; right there, on the left lotus, one should place Phena-mukha with the syllable *pheṃ*.

Nor is she who consumes food born [from a womb]; seated upon her lap is one with a blue radiance and yellowish-white eyes. Upon the lotus to her left, in the northwest on the southern lotus, one should place Vaṃjaṃ Brahmadhvani.

One should visualize the letter *phuṃ*, from which is born the face of Brahmā, smiling; seated upon his lap is the goddess Raktāvandhuragātrī, with wide eyes and the radiance of red light. There, upon the lotus to the right [of the central deity], one should visualize the letter *tasyāka*, from which is born the yellow Bhīmanādaka, who utters terrifying sounds. Upon the lotus to the left of that [Brahmā], one should visualize the letter *baṃ*, from which is born the goddess Brahmaghoṣā, smiling;
seated upon her lap is the goddess Raktābandhudehā, with a body like that of a kinsman. There, upon the lotus to her left—
And seated upon his lap was Bhaṃbījā, whose hair was like bees; she beheld in the sky the seed-syllable Haṃ, born from the syllable Ja, dark blue in color and most brilliantly radiant.

She who has the sound of terrifying laughter, dwelling upon his lap, is Puṅgava from the seed-syllable Bhaṃ; Khaḍgī, born from the seed-syllable Haṃ, is great and blue in color, blazing with light, adorned with four arms holding a wheel, a sword, a mace, and a conch, her body beautified by a crown of matted hair—one should place Hari at the eastern gate.
Adorned with four arms holding a wheel, a sword, a staff, and a conch, and beautified by limbs crowned with a diadem of swords, Viṣṇu is to be placed at the eastern gate.
To his right side, one should place Lakṣmī, whose seed-syllable is *la*, who is yellow, wears a crown and fine garments, and holds the gestures of fearlessness and a lotus.
On her right side, one should place the glorious lady from the seed-syllable LAṂ; she is yellow, with her hair tied up high, holding the gesture of fearlessness and a lotus.
Vārāhī is emanated by the syllable VAṂ on the left; she has a wrathful form, a face emitting a roar, and is radiant with a crown of skulls.
To the left of Viṣṇu is Vārāhī, manifested from the syllable Baṃ; she has the face of a sow and a wrathful form, adorned with a crown of skulls.
She is blue in color and possesses great flames, and she is fond of wearing yellow garments. In her left hand she holds a red skull-cup, and in her right she carries a severed head.
Greatly blazing with blue color, she delights in wearing yellow garments; in her left hand is a skull-cup of blood, and in her right she holds a human head.

At the northern gate is Brahmāṇī, yellow in color and most radiant, born from the seed-syllable OṂ, adorned with a crown of matted locks. At the northern gate is Brahmā, greatly blazing with yellow color, born from the seed-syllable OṂ, adorned with a crown of matted locks.
She has four arms and four faces; in her left hands she holds a lotus and a water-pot, while all her right hands hold the gesture of granting boons and a rosary.

To the four-armed [deity] with four faces, holding a lotus and a water-pot in his left hands, and a *dakṣiṇa* (gift-bestowing gesture) and a rosary in his right hands— on the right side of Brahmā is Brahmāṇī, possessing a golden luster, born from the seed-syllable BAṂ, and holding a lotus and a fly-whisk.

On the right side of Brahmā is Sarasvatī, who possesses the excellence of gold; born from the seed-syllable BAṂ, she holds a lotus and a fly-whisk. On the left side of Brahmā is Sarasvatī, green in luster; born from the seed-syllable SAṂKĀRA, she holds a red lotus in her left hand.
On the left side of Brahmā is Sarasvatī, with the luster of a jackal; born from the seed-syllable *sa*, she holds a fresh utpala lotus in her left hand.
Born from the seed-syllables *haṃ* and *śaṃ*, she is radiant with a white complexion. At the western door of Īśāna, she shines forth with four arms.
Arisen from the seed-syllables *hūṃ*, *daṃ*, and *shaṃ*, the Bhūta is white in color and blazing; he resides at the western door of Īśvara, adorned with four arms.

He holds a banner and a hand-drum in his right hands, and a trident and a skull-cup in his left; his body is covered within by a tiger skin, his matted locks are adorned with a crescent moon, and his face is resplendent with three eyes.

In his right [hands] he holds a banner and a *cang te'u* lute; in his left, a spear and a skull-cup. He wears a tiger-skin upper garment draped over his shoulders, and his hair is bound with a crescent moon as a crown. His face is adorned with three eyes.
On the right side of Hara is Maheśvarī, born from the seed-syllable *māṃ*; she is white in color, possesses three eyes, and holds a rosary and the three jewels.
On the right side of Hara is Maheśvara, born from the seed-syllable *maṃ*; he is white in color, three-eyed, and holds a rosary and a trident.
On the left side of Īśvara is Gaṅgā, born from the seed-syllable *gaṃ*; she resembles a conch, jasmine, or the moon, and holds the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and a water jar.
On the left side of Īśvara is the seed-syllable Gaṃ, from which Gaṅgāmā appears; she holds a conch and a *kunda* flower, resembling the moon, and carries a sacrificial offering and a lotus.
From the seed-syllable Saṃ arises Samudbhavā, brilliant and white in color like semen. At the southern gate is Śakra, adorned with three eyes.
Indra is at the southern gate, perfectly arisen from the seed-syllable *ŚAṂ*. He is white in color, greatly radiant, and adorned with three eyes.

With a graceful posture resting on his left hip, he holds a vajra drawn toward his heart and a jewel parasol in his right hand, while an *utpala* lotus is held in his left hand; he is beautified by a jeweled crown.

By drawing [her] to the heart with the right [hand], she holds a precious jewel parasol and is adorned with a priceless crown; in her right hand is an *utpala*, and with the left she embraces [the deity] while sporting.
To the right of Śakra is Indrāṇī, who is of beautiful white complexion; with her right hand she holds a parasol, and with her left she holds a vajra.
On the right side of Śakra is white Indrāṇī, born from the syllable *maṃ*; she holds a parasol in her right hand and embraces [him] with her left while holding a vajra.
On the horse to the left of Śakra is Trilottamā, born from the syllable *triṃ*; she is yellow, holds a staff in her left hand, and carries a goad in her right.

On the left side of Indra is the supreme bindu arising from the seed-syllable *Taṃ*; she is yellow, embracing [him], with a sacrificial post in her left hand and holding a hook (*aṅkuśa*) with her right. In the northeast and the southeast corners are yellow *Indrāṇī* and *Īśānī*, both born from the syllable *I*. They draw in all [beings] with a vajra at their hearts, in a playful posture with their left hands placed upon his lap.
In the east is *Indra*, born from the syllable *Ai*; he is yellow, with his right hand drawn back toward his heart holding a vajra, and his left hand drawn back as he embraces [his consort] in play.

One should place the goddess named Pakṣatisamāsaja, who has arisen from the syllable *ja*, on the right side of Indra. On the left is Rambhavā; Rambhā and Śyāmā are equal to the Mistress (Īśvarī). One should arrange them on the right of Indra. To his left, born from the syllable *raṃ*, is Ārambhā, who is dark blue.
Mandāravā holds a mirror in her hand; she is known by the seed-syllable *dhaṃ*. Kuvera is in the southeast corner;

*skra ni manda ra ba 'phyang* (the one with the hair-tuft, Mandara, and the banner). Holding a mirror in her hand, born from the seed-syllable *kuṃ*, is the body of Vaiśravaṇa in the south-eastern direction.

In her left hand she holds a yellow creeper, and in her right a red citron fruit. To the right of Kubera is Vasumati, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, yellow in color, and holding a golden vessel. She is radiant with a yellow creeper and a tree; in her right hand is a citron fruit. On the right side of Vaiśravaṇa is Vasumati, born from *vaṃ*, yellow in color, and possessing the intellect of wealth.

In the place of the burnt offering, Bhairava is white and blue in color; there are also goddesses with fierce forms, blue, white, yellow, and red.

In the southwest is Jara-tītā (She Who Has Transcended Old Age), with a complexion that is black and red; she is not the goddess Kapālinī. She is red, black, white, and yellow.
Vināyaka, however, is in the northwest; his color is reddish-yellow. The goddesses [beginning with] Khaḍgahastā are red, blue, white, and yellow. (8)
Regarding the drawing forth of the wind in reverse: yellow in color and possessing a yellow hue, the goddesses with swords in their hands and so forth are red, blue, white, and yellow.
And all the heroes are four-armed, bestowing skulls and drops; with their other two hands, they hold a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
The heroes have four peaceful hands; they bestow the drops from skull-cups. With the other two hands, they hold a spear and a khaṭvāṅga.
The goddesses, beginning with Cāmuṇḍī, hold tridents and vessels for drinking; four of them have swords in their hands and others are equipped with their respective weapons.
The goddesses such as Jṛmbhakī and the others hold tridents and vessels in their hands; the four beginning with Khaḍgahastā are each endowed with their respective weapons.
All should be known as seated upon corpses, adorned with ornaments of human bone; they are of terrifying form, possessed of great splendor, and resplendent with three eyes.
One should know him as possessing the flavor of all; adorned with ornaments of human bone, he has a terrifying form and great majesty, and is beautifully embellished with three eyes.
Having fully accomplished the wheel of the pledge, one should meditate upon the mandala of gnosis; having seen the mandala in space, one should cause the mandala of gnosis to descend.
Having perfected the maṇḍala of the samaya, one should meditate on the wisdom maṇḍala; with the mind, one should behold the wisdom maṇḍala as being within the space of the sky.
One should perform the rites of summoning and so forth according to the very procedure previously described, especially for all deities and worldly beings.
By means of the very same ritual previously described, one should perform the summoning and other rites for all the deities, and especially for those of the mundane world.
Having firmly bound the moon-fist (*candramuṣṭi*), with the three impurities (*trimala*) raised upward; on the third joint of the third [finger], one should place the *locanā* [seal].
Having firmly bound the moon-fist, with the three impurities raised upward, one should apply the *locanā* on the third joint of the group of the third impurity.
Oṃ ākarṣaṇi hūṃ phaṭ!
oṃ āḥ karṣaya hūṃ phaṭ | This is the mantra for the mudrā of attracting worldly deities.
The mudrā and mantra for summoning worldly deities.
One should provide a seat for the gods who have arrived; having joined the two hands together, one should open them in the shape of a lotus.
Having invited the deities, one should offer them seats; having joined the two hands together, they should be separated in the manner of a lotus.
Oṃ, abide on the seat, hūṃ svāhā!
oṃ tiṣṭha āsane hūṃ svāhā | This is the mantra for the seat mudrā.
The mudrā and mantra of the seat.

Having meditated on a white vajra in the heart, situated in the center of a moon mandala, one should display the samaya-mudrās arising from the vajra-binding. One should visualize a white vajra in the heart; it is to be beheld within the center of the moon mandala. The samaya-mudrās arise from the vajra-binding.
Placing the left fist at the heart, one should thrust the right [fist] into the armpit. This shall be the common samaya for all those belonging to the maṇḍala.
*Place the left fist at the heart; thrust the right into the armpit. This is the common samaya for all maṇḍalas.*
Oṃ hūṃ haḥ! Abide by the pledge! From this moment on, hūṃ baṃ hoḥ! You are the pledge; I am the pledge.

oṃ hūṃ hāḥ | samayati siddhiṃ draśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having joined [the hands] with the lotus-gesture (*padmajñāna*), the earth-parasol (*bhūcchatra*) is pressed down; with the two [thumbs], the middle of the chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) is formed, while the three banners (*tripatākā*) are raised.
The lotus and wisdom are joined; the earth and the parasol are pressed down by consciousness. Having bound the two with iron chains, the remaining three banners are raised high.
The three impurities and smoke should be applied; this is considered the observance (samaya) of the Lord.
The application of the three smells as incense is declared to be the commitment (samaya) of the Protector.
Oṃ X Yogāmbara, visible one! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the pledge; I am the pledge. Oṃ hūṃ haḥ svāhā!

oṃ yo gāmbhīryadṛśaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham oṃ hūṃ haḥ svāha | Having firmly bound the vajra-bind, the three impurities rise as smoke; she is renowned as Sattvavajrī, declared to be the personal samaya of the Goddess.
Having firmly bound the vajra-bind, the three impurities rise upward as smoke; she is renowned as Sattvavajrī; this is declared to be the personal samaya of the Goddess.
Oṃ! Yogāmbarī, behold! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the commitment; I am the commitment.
oṃ yo gāmbhīrīdṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | Having placed them within the vajra-bind, they are joined by primordial wisdom and consciousness.
Within the vajra-bind, primordial wisdom and consciousness are joined and established.
Oṃ vajraḍākinī! Behold! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the pledge; I am the pledge.
oṃ vajradākinyi dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Having raised up primordial wisdom and discerning awareness, she is considered the most formidable Dākinī.
That very [wisdom] elevates gnosis and consciousness; this is explained as the fierce ḍākinī.
Oṃ ghora-dākinī dṛśya [etc. | Oṃ ghoradākinī dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Padmābhūcchatrā and Sūcī are indeed the Vetālī and Dākinī.
That very lotus and the parasol [are] joined at the tips; they belong to the ḍākinī Vetālī.
Oṃ, Vetāla, Dākinī, look! and so forth.

oṃ vetālī dākinye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Having formed the vajra-bond and [visualized] the triple-streaked smoke-sign, establishing it in the form of a jewel— this is considered the *samaya* of Caṇḍālī.
Having firmly performed the vajra-binding, one joins the three with compassion; abiding in the form of a jewel, this is explained as the samaya of Caṇḍālī.
Oṃ caṇḍā-caṇḍāra-dākinī dṛśya, etc.

oṃ caṇḍālīdākinyi dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Having firmly bound the vajra-band, the white chain of the eye— this mudrā taught by the Lord is considered the *samaya* of Siṃhinī.
Having firmly performed the vajra-binding, one should join the white *gīwang*. This is the mudrā spoken by the Protector; it is the eight commitments (*samaya*) of Siṃhī.
Oṃ, O Siṃhadākinī, you who are visible, and so forth.

oṃ siṃ ha dākini driśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Having bound that very mudrā—the three impurities, smoke, and pure—one slightly opens the needle; this is proclaimed as the tiger mudrā (vyāghrimudrā).
Having stabilized that very mudrā, one joins the three scents at the tips; this joining of the tips, slightly opened, is renowned as the tiger’s mudrā.
Oṃ, O Vyāghradākinī, you who are visible, and so forth.

oṃ jyā ghrā dākini dr̥śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having firmly bound that very mudrā— the parasol, lotus, and chain— the mudrā taught by the Lord is considered the Jambukhādakasamaya.

Having firmly bound that very mudrā, one should form the earth, the parasol, the lotus, and the iron chain; these are the mudrās spoken by the Protector, and thus the samaya of Ce-spyang-ma is explained.
Oṃ jambukī dṛśya jaḥ, and so forth.
oṃ jaṃ bukkaḍākinīdr̥śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham ||
Having firmly bound the vajra-bandha, one should perform the supreme threefold expansion.
Having firmly bound the vajra-binding, one should release it three times.
Oṃ ulukinī dṛśya, and so forth.
oṃ au lū kha dākini driśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having formed the vajra-bond, one should cause it to open before the face.
Having firmly bound the vajra-union, open it wide and place it within the mouth. [Oṃ] Ḍākinī dṛśya, and so forth.
oṃ dākini dr̥śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having formed the vajra-añjali at the crown of the head, this is considered the *dīpinī-samaya*.
Placing the palms joined at the crown of the head is explained as the samaya of the butter lamp.
[Oṃ] Dīpinī, Dṛśyā, and so forth.
oṃ dīpanidṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | One should cast the *añjali* of the *preta*s into their mouths; they are considered to be the *cūṣiṇī* pledges (*samaya*).
The hungry ghost is made to join his palms; thus the commitment of Jīvamātṛ is explained.
Oṃ, O Sucker, O Visible One, and so forth.

oṃ tsu śi ni dri shya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham | Having performed the vajra-binding through the yoga of the support of the deluded, and having acted as if striking down at the front, this is considered the *samaya* of Kambojī.
Having firmly established the vajra-binding, one should join [the hands] like holding a pestle; this is explained as the samaya of Hārītī, which produces the sound of a horse.
Oṃ! O Kambojī, you who are visible! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! You are the pledge; I am the pledge! Haṃ.

oṃ kaṃ poḍi drīśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samastvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having extended [the hands], one should touch the sun and moon with the consciousness of the *bhaṅga*; these are the pledges (*samaya*) of the goddesses beginning with Pukkasī, as proclaimed by the Sage.
The sun and the moon are extended; fear and consciousness are joined. The three goddesses, Gandhāri and the others, were declared by the Sage to be the samaya.
Oṃ pukkasi dṛśya, etc.
oṃ pukkasi dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ drāmidī dṛśya, etc.
oṃ do mbi n’i drī śya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ candrī dṛśya, etc.

oṃ caṇḍālīdṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | Having extended the moon-hand and joined the sun-hand in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), this shall be the pledge (*samaya*) for the goddesses beginning with Ghorī and the others.
When the hand of the Moon is extended, it is correctly joined with the hand of the Sun; thus, the three goddesses, Raudrī and the others, become the samaya.
[Oṃ] Ghorinī, having been seen, and so forth.
oṃ gauri nīdrī śyā jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ rudhirāṇī dṛśya, etc.
oṃ ru dhira nī dri shya dzaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ samaya stvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ māṃsī dṛśya ityādi ||

oṃ maṃ śrīdṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having joined the vajra-añjali and opened it like a lotus vessel, one should display the fierce, blazing, and terrifying *ugrījvalitābhīṣaṇī* samaya.
Having firmly joined the vajra palms, one should separate them like a lotus vessel; this supreme samaya should be viewed as fierce, blazing, and formidable.
Oṃ, O fierce one (*ugre*), who art visible, and so forth.
oṃ au gī dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ jvalite dṛśya, etc.
oṃ jvala tiṣṭha dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ bhūme dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ bhi mā drī śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ samayo ’ham | This is considered the back-vajra-añjali mudrā for the three goddesses beginning with Kapālī.
The three goddesses, Thod and the others, are explained as joining their vajra palms behind their backs.
Oṃ, Kapālin, you who are visible, and so forth.
oṃ ka p’a li dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ vajriṇi dṛśya, etc.
oṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ kuśbhī dṛśya śyetyādi ||
oṃ kuṃ bhī dri śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having placed the vajra-bind at the heart, wisdom and discernment are raised aloft.
[18] The vajra-bind is joined at the heart; wisdom and discernment are raised upward.
Oṃ vajralāsye dṛśya, and so forth.
oṃ vajra lāsye dr̥śya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having placed the vajra-bond at the heart and extending it, [there is] the application of perfume.
Place the vajra-bond at the heart, extend it fully, and anoint it with fragrance: *oṃ vajragandhe dṛśya* and so forth.
oṃ vajragandhe drā śrī jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham | Having performed the vajra-binding, the lute is held in the left hand.
Having made the vajra-binding firm, place it to the left like a lute;
*oṃ vajravīṇe dṛśya* and so forth.
oṃ vajrabimbīdṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | The seal of the flower is the pledge-seal (samayamudrā), formed by the transformation of the vajra-añjali.
Having opened the vajra palms, one scatters flowers with the samaya mudrā.
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe dṛśya, and so forth.
oṃ vajrapuṣpe dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham | Having raised the vajragandha, [the practitioners] sing the songs of the white practitioners.
Raising the vajra-binding gesture upward, one sings while moving a white [object].
Oṃ vajragīte dṛśya... and so forth.
oṃ vajragīti driśya jaḥ | hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | O Vajrabandha, because you have offered incense below, it is considered the *samaya*.
The vajra-bond is presented below; it is explained as the commitment of incense.
Oṃ vajradhūpe dṛśya, etc.
oṃ vajra dhūpe driśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samaya oṃ hūṃ | Dancing with the vajra-añjali at the crown of the head is considered the samaya of Nṛtyā.
When the vajra palms meet at the crown of the head, the samaya of Gaurī arises.
Oṃ vajranṛtye dṛśya, and so forth.
oṃ vajranīti-dṛṣṭyā jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham | Having performed the vajra-binding, the right thumb is raised upward.
Having firmly formed the vajra-binding, raise the right thumb upward.
Oṃ vajradīpe dṛśya, and so forth.

oṃ vajradīpe dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samaya oṃ hūṃ | The *sattvavajrī* is prescribed for Kalaṅkabhairava and the others. Having performed the *vajrabandha* and opened it like a lotus vessel, this is the *samaya-mudrā* proclaimed for the goddesses Kamalākārī and the rest.

One should perform the ritual of Vajracitta for Keng rus, ’Jigs byed, and so forth; having firmly established the vajra-bind (vajrabandha), one should separate [the fingers] like a lotus vessel for the goddesses such as Padmarūpā and the others.
Oṃ Karaṅkabhairava, you who are visible, and so forth.
oṃ karaṃ gaurī-vadriśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ kamalākari dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ kamalākari dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ kha[ṭvāṅga]rākṣasa dṛśya, etc.
oṃ kha tvam ga rakṣasaṃ dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ kharanakhi dṛśya, etc.
oṃ kharanakhaṭri śyajaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ gambhīranāda dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ gaṃ bhiranādṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'ham | oṃ gadbharanīdanīya(! dṛśyeti-ādi ||
oṃ gaṃ bhīranāṅganye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ ghaṇṭāraṇa dṛśya, etc.
oṃ ghaṇṭakarana dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham || 4 || [oṃ] "O you who are visible as Ghaṇṭastanī," and so forth. || 4 ||
oṃ caṇḍastanidrīśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ caṇḍeśvaryai dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ caṇḍīśvari dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ caparānana dṛśya, etc. || 5 ||
oṃ tsapa l’a na n’a dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ cchitraghoṇe dṛśya, etc.
oṃ tstshitra ghona dṛśya jaḥ; hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ chidramanīye dṛśya, etc. || 6 ||
oṃ tṣṭhī tra de śa nī dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | [oṃ] for the one dear to those born from a womb, it is seen, and so forth.
oṃ vajra jvalayojapriyadṛṣṭyajāḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ jaghanonnatīye dṛśyeti etc. || 7 ||
oṃ jra ghana unna ta dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ jhaṃkārabhīravāya dṛśya śyetyādi ||
oṃ jhakharabherava dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ jhṛkṣatakāminī dṛśya, etc. || 8 ||
oṃ jhakrīta kāmamīḍṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ ṭṭiṭṭibhānu dṛśya, etc.
oṃ tiṭṭa bha śa dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ ṭikabhūṣaṇīye dṛśya, etc. || 9 ||
oṃ tika bhu śaniye driśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ ṭhāvarāgāya dṛśyety ādi ||
oṃ thi par g’a ya drī śya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ ṭhakikāminīye dṛśya ityādi || 10 ||
oṃ thikka kha minīye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ ḍamaruḍāmara dṛśya, etc.
oṃ da ma ru d’a ma ra dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ ḍiṇḍimapriyāya dṛśya ityādi || 11 ||
oṃ diṇḍi ma prīya dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ ḍhaṅkakolāhala dṛśya, etc.
oṃ dhakka ko l’a ya ha la dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ dhakkalālasīya dṛśyeti-ādi || 12 ||
oṃ dha kka l’a la s’i ye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ taṅkapriyāya dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ taṃ ka prī yāya dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ tanujaghane dṛśye, etc. || 13 ||
oṃ tannujaṃghānīye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ thoravāharāya dṛśya, etc.
oṃ thotrapāṇikhādyadṛśyajaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ tharagīnā dṛśya, etc. || 14 ||
oṃ thāranādini dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’ham | oṃ daṃṣṭrākalālinī dṛśya, etc.
oṃ daṃ śṭhā karāli dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ daradarśine dṛśya ityādi || 15 ||
oṃ daradarśanīye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ dhikkāra-ghora-dṛśyetyādi ||
oṃ dhīra ghona driśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ dhīrabhāṇīya dṛśya ityādi || 16 ||
oṃ dhīra bhāṣiṇīye dhīḥ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo ’ham | oṃ piṇḍa calācala dṛśya ityādi ||
oṃ piṇḍacāra dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ piṅgalākṣīye dṛśya, etc. || 17 ||
oṃ piṃ gala kṣmī driśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo 'haṃ | oṃ phenamukhāya driśya, etc.
oṃ phe na mu kh’a ya drīśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ phullanayanīye dṛśya etc. || 18 || [19] oṃ phulla naya n’i ye drīśya jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ samayo ’haṃ |
Oṃ, [it is] seen in the *Brahmasvane*, beginning with "dṛśya," and so forth.
oṃ brahma-dhvan-i-dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ bandhuragātrīye dṛśya ityādi || 19 ||
oṃ baṃ dhunagātraye dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | oṃ bhīmanāda dṛśya, etc.
oṃ bhrīm ānanda dṛśya jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvam | samayo 'ham | oṃ bhrāmaka-keśin dṛśya, etc. || 20 ||
oṃ bhramarakeśini dṛśya jaḥ | hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ | samayas tvaṃ | samayo ’haṃ | Having firmly bound the vajra-band, one should display the form of a wheel.

One should contemplate the pledge beings and the gnosis beings as having become one.
One should visualize the commitment being and the wisdom being as having become one.
Having meditated on the supreme syllable of Dharma fixed upon the lotus-petal of the tongue, one becomes the Dharma-mudrā through that aforementioned utterance of the mantra.
Upon the petals of the lotus of the tongue, one should visualize the supreme syllables of the Dharma; reciting the secret mantra as before constitutes the Dharma-mudrā.

[The two mantras for the upper and lower *yas-rgya* seals below have not been reconciled and are left for further investigation. *śaṃ māṃ gaṃ śaṃ māṃ tiṃ aiṃ baṃ haṃ | kuṃ paṃ saṃ | khaṃ raṃ laṃ | bhūr bhu va | bhaṃ auṃ*. These are the *dharmamudrā*.
One should visualize a universal vajra situated within a moon disc in the heart; one should employ the action seal (karmamudrā) arising from the vajra-bind.
Abiding in the form of a moon at the heart, one should meditate on the variegated vajra. As for the performance of the action mudrā, it arises from the two vajra-bindings.
Extending the moon-hand to the edge of the ear with the other [hand]: OṂ KṢUṂ. Having grasped the skull-cup with the moon-hand and placed it upon the shoulder with the right hand: OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ. 1.
The Moon holds the skull-cup; in the right hand is the Khaṭvāṅga. Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
Having formed a gesture of salutation with joined palms, one should open them into the shape of a lotus. Oṃ Āḥ Aḥ. 2.
Having performed the salutation and joined the palms, one should perform the differentiation of the lotus: OṂ ĀḤ ĀḤ.
Having joined Bhūcchatrā and Viṣṭajñā, she becomes the Vajriṇī in the form of a three-pronged needle: OṂ SUṂ SAḤ. 2.
One should join the parasol with consciousness; the three-pronged vajra should be fashioned. Oṃ Suṃ Saḥ!

One should unite the consciousness resting upon the earth-parasol with the lotus through gnosis. Having placed [the syllables] Oṃ Bhā Bhāṃ behind [it], one becomes the Vajriṇī raised up by the remainder. Kṣuṃ Kṣuṃ. 3.
On the parasol, one relies upon consciousness; the lotus is joined with primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Having purified the seal of both, the remaining [deity] is Vajrī standing upright: *oṃ kṣuṃ kṣaḥ*.
That very [deity] is Vetālī-Dākinī, facing backward and behind, with a mute mouth: *yuṃ yaḥ*. 4.

That very [seal] expanded is the one facing forward; it is the *vetāḍī-dākinī-mudrā*. Having formed the *vajra-muṣṭi*, with white eyes raised and holding [the hand] in the form of a jewel, this becomes the *caṇḍālikā-mudrā*. Oṃ hūṃ ha. 5.
Having made firm the two vajra-fists, with the white [thumb] and the index finger raised upward, they are joined in the manner of a jewel; this becomes the mudrā of Caṇḍālī. OṂ HŪṂ HAḤ.
Having formed the two vajra-fists, with the white eye and the cord [raised]: OṂ SMRYUṂ. 6.
Forming two vajra-fists, one should join the white index fingers. OṂ SMRYUṂ. Having bound that very same mudrā, [it is] Trimalā Dhūmaśūcikā. OṂ HRYUṂ. 7.
Having bound that very mudrā, [one forms] the three scents with the tips joined like smoke: Oṃ Hūṃ Rūṃ.
Having thus bound that mudrā, there is the Earth-Umbrella and the Lotus-Chain: Oṃ Ymr[y]ūṃ. 8.
Having bound that very mudrā, one should manifest the earth-parasol and the lotus. Oṃ ymryūṃ.
Having formed the vajra-fist, the supreme triple-emission is performed: Oṃ kṣmr[y]ūṃ. [20] 9.
Having firmly bound the vajra in the hollowed-palm gesture, one should express enthusiasm toward the directions three times: OṂ KṢMRYŪṂ.
Having placed both hands in the mouth: OṂ PHŪṂ PHEṂ. 10.
Place both hands into the mouth; *oṃ phuṃ phaṃ*.
Having placed the *añjali* at the crown of the head: *oṃ pheṃ pheṃ*. 11.
Placing the palms joined together at the crown of the head: OṂ PHAṂ PHAṂ.
One should cast the *preta*-añjali into the mouth: OṂ PHOṂ PHĪṂ. 12.
The hungry ghost (preta) raises its palms toward the mouth. OṂ PHROṂ PHAṂ.
Having firmly formed the left fist, one should hold it at the root of the ear. OṂ PHIṂ. 13.
Firmly binding the left fist, one should grasp it at the root of the ear. OṂ PHRIṂ PHAṂ.
One should cause the nectar situated in the hand of the Sun to be given by the one who knows the [proper] method. OṂ HAḤ HOḤ HRĪḤ. 2(?).

The Sun’s Hand (Sūryahasta) abides in nectar; he is devoid of fear and consciousness. OṂ HA HO HRĪḤ | [He] stands upon Candra and Aṅkuśapāla, with his right hand in the gesture of fearlessness. OṂ GHRĪṂ GHRAṂ || 3 ||
The moon rests upon a skull-hook; with her right hand she grants fearlessness. Oṃ ghīṃ ghraḥ, both hands hold a vessel for offerings. Oṃ kuru 2. 3.
With both hands like offering bowls: *oṃ kuru kuru*.
With the hand of the sun, one partakes of the foods and edibles situated upon the moon: *oṃ vattari vattari*. 3(?).
One should abide in eating, chewing, and savoring; one should eat with the hand of the sun. Oṃ battāli battāli.
One should hold both fists at the sides of the waist in the *candrasūrya* [mudrā]. Oṃ hūṃ. 1.
The two fists of the moon and sun should be held on the side of the elbow. OṂ HŪṂ.
Having extended the moon-hand and joined it with the knowledge of the frowning brow, one should grasp it with the sun-hand and smear it with the fragrance mudrā. OṂ SUPRIYAGANDHE HŪṂ. 2.
Extending the hand of the Moon, one should join it with *bhī* and *vijñāna*; having grasped it with the hand of the Sun, one should apply the fragrance-mudrā. OṂ SUPRIYAGANDHE HŪṂ.
Having formed a scissor with the left hand, arising in the shape of a lute, and raising it with the hand of the Sun, she is intent upon playing the lute. OṂ HŪṂ HOḤ.
Forming the curved knife gesture with the left hand, raise the *vīṇā* upward; slightly warmed by the rays of the sun, that *vīṇā* is the supreme among sounds. OṂ HŪṂ HOḤ.
Having formed the *sūryamuṣṭi*, one should join it with the white [deity] through gnosis (*jñāna*). Extending the remaining fingers, this is proclaimed as the flower mudrā. OṂ ŚRIṂ. 4.

Having firmly formed the *sūryamukha-muṣṭi* (sun-fist), one joins the white [thumb] with the *jñāna* [thumb]; the remaining fingers are extended upward. This is renowned as the *puṣpa-mudrā* (flower gesture). *oṃ śrī sūryamukhi samādhāya hūṃ*. Having uttered the syllable *hūṃ*, the white [thumb] is moved at the tip of the mouth; this is proclaimed as the *gītā-mudrā* (song gesture). *oṃ hūṃ haṃ haṃ*. 5.
Having firmly formed the solar fist (sūryamuṣṭi) and uttering the syllable HŪṂ, one moves the white [substance] at the tip of the mouth; this is renowned as the mudrā of Gaurī. OṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ.
Having formed the solar fist, one holds incense and fumigates; OṂ AḤ. 6.
Having made firm the Sūryamuṣṭi (Sun-fist), place the smoke upward like incense; OṂ AIḤ.
Then, one should cast the left hand onto the right hip; the Sūryahasta (Sun-hand) is held aloft in a well-established dancing posture. OṂ SUNṚTYE HŪṂ. 7.
On the right side of the waist, the left hand should be raised; with the sun-like hand pointing upward, one should stand well in the manner of a dancer. *oṃ su nr̥te hūṃ*.
Having firmly raised the *sūryamuṣṭi* (sun-fist), the thumb therein should be well-erected; this shall be the *dīpamudrā* (lamp-seal) for him, illuminating all worlds. *oṃ kṣuṃ*. 8.
Raising the *sūryamuṣṭi* (sun-fist) upward, with the thumb extended upward, it becomes the mudrā of the lamp that illuminates the entire world. OṂ KṢU.
Holding a trident with both hands, joined with the consciousness of destruction (*bhaṅgavijñāna*), this is proclaimed as the *karmamudrā* of Karaṅka, Bhairava, and the others. KAṂ KAḤ. 1.
The terrifying one is joined with consciousness; the moon-hand holds the trident. This is renowned as the activity mudrā of Kaṅkāla-bhairava and the others: Oṃ kaṃ ka.

Having joined the palms in *añjali* with both hands, one should expand them like a skull-cup (*kapāla*). The right arm is raised upward; with the left, it is joined in front. OṂ KHE ŚA HAṂ.
Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* mudrā, one performs the opening like a lotus. OṂ LAṂ LAḤ.
Having formed the joined palms, open them wide like a lotus: OṂ LAṂ BAṂ.
Having bound the hollowed-añjali, one should open it like a skull-cup: OṂ VĀṂ VA.
Having bound the palms together, one should analyze [the mantra] according to what has been heard:
*oṃ va-vyañjanaṃ* (or *vyañjanam*) by means of the "sun-hand" (*sūryahasta*), through the application of the moon and sun. *oṃ oṃ*.
The hand of the Sun is the fan; it should be joined to the body of the Moon. Oṃ Āṃ | To Lakṣmī and Mudrā, who are devoted to Brahmā: Oṃ Braṃ Va.
The mudrā of Śrī is Brahmāṇī...

[joining the hands in] the *saṃpuṭa-añjali*, from which the three impurities are gathered like smoke; white, with eyes closed, and joined together—this is considered the mudrā of Sarasvatī. Oṃ saṃ saḥ. 2.
Having bound the palms together, with the three scents, smoke, and touch, and the union of white [sandalwood] and *gīvaṅga*, this is explained as the mudrā of Sarasvatī. OṂ SAṂ SAḤ.
Having joined with the lotus-wisdom (*padmā-jñāna*), one holds a trident raised from the remainder. OṂ HŪṂ SAḤ.
The lotus and wisdom are joined; the remainder are held upright, grasping tridents. OṂ HŪṂ SA | Bhūcchatrā is embraced by Vijñāna, while the rest hold tridents raised aloft. OṂ MĀṂ MA ||
He joins the parasol with consciousness; the remaining [fingers] are raised upward like short spears. Oṃ māṃ maḥ | Lakṣmīsūdreva from the Gaṅgā | Gaṃ ga || 3 ||

Regarding the *gaṃgala* mudrā of Śrī: having formed the left fist at the heart, one should extend the index finger over a yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and place it there. It should be like a leaf of the *subhā* plant. *Oṃ su mu hūṃ*.

Form a fist with the left hand at the heart; extend the index finger upward and place it there. It becomes like a sun or a parasol. Oṃ śamu hūṃ | bhūcchatra vijñāsaṃśleṣā śeṣam ucchrita-vajriṇī | oṃ iṃ iḥ ||
He joins the parasol with consciousness; the remaining [fingers] are raised upward as a vajra. Oṃ aiṃ aiḥ.
Having formed the *sūryamuṣṭi* (sun-fist), the white [finger] is curled and drawn in. Oṃ tiṃ ti. 4.

Having firmly bound the "Sun Fist" (*sūryamuṣṭi*), one should summon the White One. OṂ TIṂ TI. The Sun Fist is placed on the forehead; the two fingers are white and smoky, bound at the eyes, and bent crosswise. This is revealed as the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*). OṂ I MU HŪṂ.
Placing the *sūryamuṣṭi* (sun-fist) at the forehead, one burns with the two [syllables] *ka* and *du*. Having bound the corners of the eyes, it is clearly manifest as the *karmamudrā*. OṂ AI MU HŪṂ.
Through the knowledge of the lotus (*padmajñāna*), there is an embrace; the rest is the raised Vajriṇī. OṂ SAṂ SA.
The lotus and wisdom are joined; the remaining [fingers] are raised upward as a vajra. Oṃ saṃ sa. With the sun-hand, a mirror: Oṃ raṃ ra. 5.
With the sun-like hand upon the surface of a mirror, [recite] *oṃ raṃ ra*.
Having formed a fist with both hands, raise up white *rocanā* (yellow pigment). Joining it in the form of a jewel, one should hold it at the location of the heart. *Oṃ dhanāgre hūṃ*.
Having firmly clenched the fists, raise the white bracelets upward; having joined the jewels together, they should be held at the position of the sun. OṂ KUNDHANA KUGGE HŪṂ.
[Grant] fearlessness with the hand of the sun. OṂ VAṂ VAḤ.
Fearless through the hand of the Sun; oṃ vaṃ vaḥ, the boon-granting one with the sun in his hand; oṃ hūṃ haḥ. 6.
The hand of the Sun performs the supreme gift (*vara-mudrā*). Oṃ haṃ ha!
Having dissolved Rocanā upward, she is white, smoke-colored, and possesses a banner (*patākinī*). Oṃ khātani hūṃ phaṭ!
Placing the ring finger upward, it is white and smoky; OṂ KHAṂ KHAṂ KHĀṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ.
This is the *samayamudrā* of Maheśvarī. OṂ LAṂ LAṂ.

Possessing the forms of glorious body, speech, and mind, with three faces displaying the sentiments of love, wrath, and laughter, and three eyes; their bodies are intensely beautiful with the luster of ruby and sapphire; their supreme arms are marked with the six symbols and they possess the six seasons.

The glorious body, speech, and mind have three faces—amorous, wrathful, and laughing—and three eyes. With the supreme wealth of the light of Indra’s *cīla*, his body is exceedingly fierce, and his hands possess the six unsurpassed [attributes].

O you who hold in your hands the skull-cup, the limb, the arrow, the knife, the thunderbolt, and the bell; O you who utter the sound "hā hā," who cut through the ocean of hands; O bestower of liberation, who grants release from the states of existence—at the pair of feet of you, Vajrajñānavara-Ḍākinī!

You hold the skull-cup, the hand-drum, the arrow, the bow, the vajra, and the bell—marked with these six insignia. Uttering the sound "ha ha," you cut through the day-maker [the sun] with your ears; though liberated from cyclic existence, you bestow the state of liberation. You are the supreme vajra wisdom; I prostrate at the feet of you, Ḍākinī!

O Śrīkāyamūrti, who today bears the color of peace, who holds a khaṭvāṅga and the supreme jewel-yoga while bearing a skull-cup, you who remove the afflictions of the great ocean of the sea of saṃsāra—homage to you, O Vajradākinī, whose pair of feet are venerated!

Your glorious body, from this day forth, shall bear a peaceful hue; together with Khaṭvāṅga, you supreme yoginī holding a skull-cup, you utterly plunder the afflictions of the great ocean of saṃsāra. You are the Vajra-Ḍākinī; I prostrate at your feet.

O Śrīratnamūrti, whose complexion alone is most enchanting; who holds a khaṭvāṅga and a vessel filled with the supreme nectar; you who comfort the bodies of many suffering beings—O terrible Ḍākinī, homage to you whose pair of feet are repeatedly saluted!

Glorious one with a precious body, Your form is exceedingly beautiful; Holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*) Filled with the supreme nectar, You bring relief to the bodies Of many beings who suffer. You are the fierce ḍākinī; I prostrate at your feet.

The one of glorious form, the embodiment of Dharma, of excellent and beautiful appearance, possessing the hue of a ruby, who holds aloft a khaṭvāṅga and carries a skull-cup filled [with nectar], who severs the bonds of existence for the entire world—homage to him whose feet are venerated by Vetālas and Ḍākinīs.

Glorious supreme Dharmakāya, with a beautiful form like a ruby, your Khaṭvāṅga is held upright; you hold a skull-cup filled with impurities. You sever the bonds of existence for all wandering beings. To you, Ḍākinī Vetālī, I prostrate at your feet.

O Śrī Karmamūrti, possessing green luster and unfailing form, who holds a fierce khaṭvāṅga and a skull filled with the nectar of mercury; you who sever the bonds of existence arising from afflictions such as passion—homage to you, whose feet are venerated by the fierce Ḍākinīs!

Glorious one, body of action, possessing meaningful form and the color of an unaging maiden, with a fierce human face and the syllable *tvaṃ*, you hold a skull-cup together [with your consort]. You sever the bonds of existence—the afflictions such as passion and the rest. To the ḍākinī Caṇḍālī, I prostrate at your feet.

With her threatening forefinger, she destroys the wicked who bear nooses and weapons; holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a goad in her right hand, she wields at the tip of her arm a supreme staff that cuts down the wicked.

The glorious and supreme Lioness and Tigeress, the Vulture-faced and the Eagle-faced—all of them brandish the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and hold the noose (*pāśa*), utterly destroying all that is hostile. With their right hands they hold the *khaṭvāṅga* and the iron hook (*aṅkuśa*); with their hands they wield the supreme staff, crushing the enemies and the malevolent ones.

You are the one who effects the destruction of the suffering of existence through separation from everything; you are Māyāduḥpinī, whose feet are worshipped by the Yakṣas. You are Dākinī, the supreme illuminator and the drinker; you are Kambojinī, the protector of the world, of fierce form.

You destroy all fetters of existence and utterly vanquish suffering; you possess an illusory form—to your feet I prostrate. You are the supreme among ḍākinīs: Dīpikā, Bhīmā, Hārī, and Pṛthivīdhara, who possesses a fierce form.

O destroyer of the wicked and unsubdued spells of others, you whose pair of feet are worshipped by all deities and dākinīs; O Lāsya, enchanting one, grant me garlands and song, with the sounds of beautiful vocal melodies and the dance of lovely women.

I bow at the feet of you, Ḍākinī, who subdues those who are difficult to tame and the malevolent, and who destroys the vidyās of others. Lāsyā, Manoharā, Manoramā, Mālā, and Gītā proclaim well-composed songs; Nṛtyā possesses limbs of extreme suppleness, and there are various kinds of flowers.

The supreme incense of various and diverse flowers, the pure lamp of the light of primordial wisdom, the fragrance of excellent perfumes; the wheel of yoga of the secret hand of the faculty of diligence, consisting of yoga, subsequent yoga, extreme yoga, and great yoga.

Incense that rises upward, the beautiful light of primordial wisdom, lamps, and fragrant perfumes—these are the supreme secret of the faculty of diligence. The wheel of yogins and yoginīs, the yoga, the subsequent yoga, the intense yoga, and the great yoga.
